title: The end of al-Hashr
tomorrow: why does a bedtime surah tell you to look at the sky again?

cards: Every contact in your phone gets one name, maybe an emoji. Nobody you love fits in it. The end of al-Hashr starts with something even bigger failing to hold up.
In Pickthall's words: "If We had caused this Qur'an to descend upon a mountain, thou (O Muhammad) verily hadst seen it humbled, rent asunder by the fear of Allah." A mountain, cracking.
And right after it, a flood of names.

teach.b: The question underneath is old: can any name hold God? The passage opens by turning to the listener: "let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow."
Then a line worth telling a friend: don't be like those who forgot God, so that He made them forget themselves. Forget God, the verse says, and you lose track of your own soul. Then the mountain.
Then the names, in a rush: "He is Allah, than Whom there is no other God, the Sovereign Lord, the Holy One, Peace, the Keeper of Faith, the Guardian, the Majestic, the Compeller, the Superb."
And: "He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner. His are the most beautiful names."
The answer here: no single name holds Him, so the names come many, each one a window, and every one of them begins with He is Allah. Now a neighbor.
In the Torah, God passes before Moses and proclaims who He is, in the JPS words: "merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth."
Jewish tradition treasures those attributes of mercy and recites them on solemn days. The shared ground: both reach for God through names of mercy. And an honest difference.
Muslims call on God by the beautiful names aloud, in prayer and dhikr. In Jewish practice, the holiest name, written with four letters, isn't spoken; readers say Adonai, my Lord, in its place.
One way honors God by calling on many names. The other honors a name by keeping it unspoken.

how: Muslims call on God by His beautiful names in personal prayer and dhikr, often counting them on prayer beads; the last verses of al-Hashr are recited in Arabic and memorized.

games.q: at dinner, Jordan's cousin, who is Jewish, says her family never says God's holiest name aloud. Amira's family calls on God's names in prayer. a fair way to put it?
o: one family must be getting it wrong.
it's all the same practice, just in different languages.
two ways of honoring: calling on many names, or keeping one unspoken.
games.why: shared ground and an honest difference: both reach for God through names of mercy; one calls on them aloud, the other guards the holiest name in silence. neither is ranked.

practice: Read the list slowly, pausing at each name: the Holy One, Peace, the Keeper of Faith, the Guardian, the Creator, the Fashioner. Then take a pen and write by hand the one that stopped you. Hold that single name through the sit.

wordCard.voice: The end of al-Hashr: the last verses of surah 59, a humbled mountain and a cascade of the most beautiful names.

carryVoice: Carry this: the most beautiful names, many windows onto one God. The list is yours now.
